spots.name: Canton Tower
spots.label: Canton Tower

text.access_note: The area around the tower is a public space you can walk to, but access to the tower's decks and attractions may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Canton Tower stands in Haizhu District, close to Haixinsha Island.
text.description:
Canton Tower is a 600-metre observation tower in Haizhu District, and it looks like nothing else on the skyline. Its lattice of columns, rings and braces twists as it rises and pinches in at about the halfway point, which is why locals nicknamed it "Slim Waist". The tower came into use in September 2010, just before the Asian Games that Guangzhou hosted that year. For a short while it was the tallest tower in the world. It was designed by Dutch architects working with the engineering firm Arup, and the twisting shape comes from rotating two ovals, one at the base and one near the top, against each other.

That shape is what makes it so photogenic. The lines of the lattice curve and cross, and the narrow waist gives your picture a natural focal point. You will probably need to tilt the phone upwards and accept that the sides lean inwards a little, which can look quite dramatic. If you want it to look straighter, step back a few paces and zoom in slightly rather than tilting more. Keep a person or a railing in the lower corner to give a sense of scale. If the tower fills the frame, try a vertical (portrait-orientation) shot.
text.directions_text: Metro and bus stations are located underground at the base of the tower, so head for the tower itself in Haizhu District. Once you are in the area, the tower is very easy to see. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the structure stays detailed. If you shoot after dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a wall to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it sits centred, or place it on one third line with space beside it. Include a little foreground, such as paving, trees or a railing, to give it depth. For a different view, try a close crop on the waist at 2x or more, where the twist is easiest to see.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in as much of the tower's height as you can from this close. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter, less stretched view of the waist. Telephoto (2x-5x) suits the detail of the lattice and the top section.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good time, as the sky colours can contrast well with the tower's shape. The tower is probably lit up in the evening, which gives night shots a different look.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Hold the phone upright and tilt it up gently.

spots.alt: Canton Tower, Guangzhou: a 600-metre observation tower in Haizhu District. Photo spot

spots.name: Shamian Island
spots.label: Shamian Island

text.access_note: The island's avenues are public pedestrian streets, but individual buildings, churches and hotels may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Shamian Island is in Liwan District, Guangzhou. It is bordered by the Pearl River to the south and separated from the mainland by a narrow canal.
text.description: Shamian Island is a small sandbank island in Guangzhou's Liwan District, and it feels very different from the busy streets around it. It covers about 0.3 square kilometres, roughly 900 m from east to west and 300 m from north to south. The Pearl River runs along its southern edge and a canal separates it from the mainland. In 1859 the island was split between Britain and France, and the old trading mansions, churches and quiet tree-lined pedestrian avenues are still there. That mix is why it photographs so well: long shaded walks, verandahed buildings in various states of repair, and bronze statues dotted around that show scenes from the island's past. Two buildings are worth looking for. Christ Church Shameen dates from 1865, and Our Lady of Lourdes Chapel was completed in 1892. The chapel stands at the French end of the island. Today the island also has hotels, restaurants and souvenir shops, so there is somewhere to stop between pictures. Look for tree-framed avenues, building facades with their verandahs, and the statues, which make good foreground subjects. Take your time, as the best shots are often found by following the quiet side streets.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best route to Shamian Island in Liwan District. Once on the island, walk to the phone icon on the map. From there the marked spot is 292 m to the west, a short walk. The island is a pedestrian-friendly place, so it is easy to explore on foot from there. The phone icon on the map is about 290 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the main subject, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright sky is washing out the buildings. In shaded avenues, hold your phone steady, and use night mode if you are shooting in dim light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up an avenue so the trees on each side frame the view and the buildings lead the eye into the picture. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the whole avenue, and keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean. For the bronze statues, get close and use portrait mode to separate them from the background. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out details such as verandahs and church facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes and building fronts. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long tree-lined avenues, and use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details and the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually pleasant, as the light is softer and the island is often quieter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.

spots.alt: Shamian Island, Guangzhou: a small sandbank island in Guangzhou's Liwan District. Photo spot

spots.name: Guangzhou Opera House
spots.label: Guangzhou Opera House

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the building are generally open to the public, but check the official site before you go, especially if you want to go inside, as interior access and photography depend on events.
text.geographic_location: In Guangzhou, with the Pearl River to the south, beside the open square of 花城广场 and its neighbouring library and museum.
text.description:
Guangzhou Opera House was designed by Zaha Hadid and opened on 9 May 2010. It was conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River, and the building does look like a pair of large pebbles, with sloping stone-clad sides and no obvious straight lines. That makes it a good subject for a phone. The shapes are bold and the outline reads clearly even in a small picture. The auditorium is concrete, set inside a granite and glass-clad steel frame, and the building took over five years to build. It is the biggest performing centre in southern China.

The best view for most visitors is from the square, 花城广场, rather than the building's own forecourt. From there the opera house sits in a row with the library and the museum, and the Canton Tower rises behind. The square is spacious, so you can fit in the whole group of buildings and often keep crowds out of the frame. If you want a closer, more abstract picture, walk over to the building itself. The double-curved stone form is reflected in the water pool in front of it, which is worth a few frames of its own.

Take a wide shot first to show the setting, then move in for the curves and the reflection. Keep the phone level so the big curves look natural rather than leaning.
text.directions_text: Go by taxi or use a map app from central Guangzhou, and search for or ask for 花城广场 or 广州大剧院 (show the Chinese names on your phone). From there the opera house is about 2 minutes on foot to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the opera house to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone and sky keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your arms against your body, or rest the phone on a ledge, to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the buildings up with a horizontal line so the curves look natural. Leave open space in the foreground to show how big the square is. If you want a different view, go to the building's own forecourt and shoot the curved stone form with its reflection in the water pool.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole row of buildings. Then use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the opera house alone. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Canton Tower behind or for the stone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good choice, as the light is softer on the stone. Early morning is likely to be quieter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 花城广场. The opera house as one part of a row with the library and museum, with the Canton Tower in the background. The opera house is to the west of you. From here you see it as one part of a row with the library and the museum, and the Canton Tower in the background.
